data.label: Head Unit OS
data.description: Linux-based RTOS (e.g., AGL / Android Automotive OS) managing process scheduling, memory, drivers, and security policy enforcement on the SoC. Runs hypervisor partitions for safety and infotainment domains.

data.label: Bluetooth/Wi-Fi Stacks
data.description: Dual-mode wireless protocol stacks supporting BT 5.2 (A2DP, HFP, AVRCP, PBAP) and IEEE 802.11ac Wi-Fi. Handles pairing, bonding key storage, RF proximity-based attacks surface, and OTA data bridging. Exposes RFCOMM and L2CAP channels.

data.label: USB Driver Stack
data.description: USB 3.0/2.0 host and device mode driver handling MTP, Android Auto, Apple CarPlay, and mass-storage enumeration. Physical port accessible to any connected device; primary vector for media injection and firmware staging attacks.

data.label: Telephony Stacks
data.description: 4G/LTE or 5G modem abstraction layer including RIL (Radio Interface Layer), SMS, voice call routing, and telematics data plane. If SIM-enabled, exposes remote SMS command injection surface and over-the-air carrier exploits.

data.label: Application Layer Code
data.description: Signed OEM application binaries running in user space: media player, maps, voice assistant, and OEM store. Code Flash equivalent — if unsigned or improperly verified, subject to arbitrary code execution via malicious app sideloading.

data.label: Navigation Data
data.description: Stored map tiles, POI databases, last-known-location history, frequently-visited destinations, and route cache. Privacy-sensitive; if exfiltrated reveals driver habits and home address. Integrity loss causes map poisoning.

data.label: PII / User Profiles
data.description: Synchronized cloud profile data including driver contact lists (PBAP), call history, SMS messages, linked accounts (Spotify/Google), biometric seat/mirror preferences, and payment tokens for toll or EV charging services.

data.label: OTA Update Client
data.description: FOTA/SOTA agent responsible for downloading, verifying (code-signature), and applying software updates over cellular or Wi-Fi. If signature verification is bypassed or the channel is MITM'd, allows persistent malicious firmware installation.

data.label: CAN Gateway
data.description: Software/hardware gateway translating infotainment requests (e.g. climate, seat, vehicle speed display) to in-vehicle CAN or LIN frames. Acts as a trust boundary — a compromised IHU can leverage this to inject off-domain CAN messages into powertrain or body networks.

data.label: Audio Amplifier
data.description: Digital Signal Processor (DSP) and Class-D power amplifier driving up to 8 speakers at rated SPL. Receives I2S/TDM audio from the SoC. Susceptible to acoustic DoS (e.g., max-volume injection) or clipping attacks that damage speakers via corrupted DSP configuration.

data.label: Cloud / OEM Backend
data.description: OEM server infrastructure hosting OTA update manifests, map data, connected-services APIs (remote start, geofence), and analytics telemetry. Compromise of the backend propagates to all fielded vehicles.

data.label: Vehicle CAN / LIN / Ethernet
data.description: In-vehicle network backbone shared with ADAS, BCM, Powertrain, and HVAC ECUs. The IHU's CAN gateway is an ingress point into this domain — lateral movement from infotainment to safety-critical ECUs is the primary systemic risk.

Derivations.name: CWE-269: Improper Privilege Management → CVE-class Root Privilege Escalation in Android Automotive OS
Derivations.loss: Unauthorized root-level code execution on the Head Unit OS
Derivations.damageScene: An attacker exploits an unpatched privilege-escalation vulnerability in the Android Automotive OS kernel or a privileged service. Obtaining root access allows disabling SELinux policies, installing persistent backdoors in /system, and laterally pivoting to the CAN gateway. The OS integrity is permanently compromised, enabling silent firmware manipulation of connected vehicle components.

Derivations.name: CVE-2020-0022 (BlueFrag) class — CWE-120: Buffer Copy without Checking Size of Input on BT Stack
Derivations.loss: Remote unauthenticated code execution via Bluetooth proximity attack
Derivations.damageScene: An attacker within ~10 m Bluetooth range sends a crafted L2CAP packet exploiting a heap overflow in the BT stack (e.g., BlueFrag-style). No user interaction or pairing is required. The attacker gains arbitrary code execution within the BT daemon context, downloads a secondary payload over Wi-Fi, and establishes a reverse shell for persistent access to the IHU.

Derivations.name: CAPEC-27: Malicious File Loading via USB — CWE-494: Download of Code Without Integrity Check
Derivations.loss: Malware installation and data exfiltration via USB-connected device
Derivations.damageScene: A rogue USB thumb drive with a crafted autorun or MTP payload is plugged into the USB port by a vehicle occupant or valet. The USB driver stack parses a malformed filesystem or MTP packet, triggering a buffer overflow. A malicious application is sideloaded to the IHU, enabling keylogging of Bluetooth PIN, reading call history, and exfiltrating navigation data to a remote server over Wi-Fi.

Derivations.name: CAPEC-161: Infrastructure Manipulation — CWE-20: Improper Input Validation in RIL / SMS Parser
Derivations.loss: Arbitrary remote code execution via silent SMS (Type-0 / binary SMS) injection
Derivations.damageScene: An attacker with access to a rogue base station or compromised carrier sends a specially crafted binary SMS (Class 0 / binary WAP-PUSH) to the vehicle's SIM number. The RIL SMS parser fails to validate message length, causing a heap overflow. The attacker achieves remote code execution on the telephony daemon without any driver action, establishing a persistent C2 channel over the LTE data plane.

Derivations.name: CWE-295: Improper Certificate Validation — MITM App Store Update leading to malicious app installation
Derivations.loss: Unsigned or trojaned application code executing in IHU user space
Derivations.damageScene: An attacker performs a MITM attack on the OEM app store update channel (e.g., poisoned DNS, rogue Wi-Fi AP). Due to improper TLS certificate pinning in the app manager, a modified application binary bypasses signature checks. The trojanized media-player app gains access to microphone, GPS, and CAN vehicle-data APIs, enabling covert surveillance and targeted CAN frame injection via the gateway.

Derivations.name: CWE-345: Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity — Map / POI Poisoning Attack
Derivations.loss: Navigation data integrity violation causing driver misdirection
Derivations.damageScene: An attacker with write access (via a compromised app or USB) modifies stored map tiles and POI databases in the IHU's flash. The navigation system silently routes the driver through roads under attacker surveillance or into dangerous areas. In fleet scenarios, bulk manipulation enables coordinated vehicle misdirection. Exfiltration of route history also discloses driver home address and daily routine.

Derivations.name: CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information — Mass PII Exfiltration via Synchronised Cloud Profile
Derivations.loss: Disclosure of driver PII contact list, call history, payment tokens, and biometric preferences
Derivations.damageScene: An attacker exploits a broken access-control vulnerability in the IHU profile-sync service to exfiltrate driver contact lists (PBAP), full call history, SMS messages, and linked payment tokens stored in the IHU's credential vault. GDPR-regulated personal data is transmitted to a remote server. In aggregate, fleet-scale exfiltration enables targeted spear-phishing and identity fraud against vehicle owners.

Derivations.name: CWE-494: Download of Code Without Integrity Check — Malicious OTA Package Installation
Derivations.loss: Persistent malicious firmware installed fleet-wide via compromised OTA channel
Derivations.damageScene: An attacker compromises the OEM cloud backend or performs a BGP-hijack of the OTA CDN. A crafted update package with a forged or replayed signature is delivered to the OTA client. Due to weak rollback-protection or signature-bypass, the IHU installs the malicious package. The attack can be delivered silently to all vehicles checking in for updates in a specific region, achieving persistent control of millions of IHUs simultaneously.

Derivations.name: ATM Technique: CAN Bus Message Injection via Compromised IHU Gateway
Derivations.loss: Injection of arbitrary CAN frames into vehicle powertrain or body network
Derivations.damageScene: After gaining control of the IHU (via BT, USB, or OTA exploit), an attacker leverages the CAN gateway's insufficient message filtering to inject crafted CAN frames targeting adjacent ECUs. This enables disabling ESC/ABS, altering HVAC, locking/unlocking doors remotely, or spoofing instrument cluster data. The IHU-to-CAN path represents the most critical lateral movement vector from the infotainment domain into safety-critical systems.

Derivations.name: CWE-1284: Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input — DSP Configuration Abuse / Acoustic DoS
Derivations.loss: Denial-of-service via maximum-volume injection or speaker damage through DSP mis-configuration
Derivations.damageScene: An attacker who has compromised the SoC/IHU OS sends a crafted DSP configuration command over the I2S/I2C control bus. The amplifier is programmed to output maximum gain at a frequency that exceeds speaker rated power, permanently damaging voice-coils. Alternatively, a rapid loud-noise burst is injected to impair driver situational awareness during critical driving manoeuvres.

scenes.Name: Cryptographic Verification of All OTA & App Updates
scenes.Description: The IHU shall verify the integrity and authenticity of every OTA package and sideloaded application using ECDSA-P256 signatures. Packages failing verification shall be rejected and logged.

scenes.Name: Bluetooth Stack Hardening — Input Validation and Memory Safety
scenes.Description: The BT protocol stack shall enforce strict length-bounds checking on all L2CAP, HFP, and A2DP packets. A memory-safe implementation (bounds-checked parser) shall be used. Regular CVE patching cadence required.

scenes.Name: USB Attack Surface Reduction
scenes.Description: The IHU USB driver stack shall enumerate only whitelisted USB device classes (Audio, HID, MTP). Mounting of unknown mass-storage filesystems in user-accessible storage paths shall be prohibited without integrity verification.

scenes.Name: CAN Gateway Strict Message Filtering
scenes.Description: The CAN gateway shall implement an allowlist of infotainment-originated CAN IDs. Any frame with a source CAN ID outside the allowed infotainment domain shall be dropped and a DTC logged.

scenes.Name: PII Encryption at Rest and in Transit
scenes.Description: All PII (contact lists, call history, SMS, payment tokens) stored on the IHU shall be encrypted at rest using AES-256-GCM with keys derived from a device-bound credential. Data in transit shall use TLS 1.3 with certificate pinning.

scenes.Name: Head Unit OS SELinux Mandatory Access Control
scenes.Description: All IHU OS processes shall run under a strictly defined SELinux policy. Privilege escalation vectors (SUID binaries, writable system paths) shall be eliminated. Policy enforcement shall be verified by automated CI security scanning.

scenes.Name: Telephony RIL Input Validation and Isolation
scenes.Description: The RIL SMS parser shall enforce maximum message length and character-set bounds. The telephony daemon shall run in an isolated sandbox (Linux namespace) with no direct access to CAN gateway or file system paths outside its domain.

scenes.Name: Navigation Data Integrity Verification
scenes.Description: Map tile packages shall include Merkle-tree hash manifests signed by the OEM map provider. The navigation application shall verify these hashes before committing tile updates to persistent storage.

scenes.Name: [CS-IHU-R1] Enforce TLS 1.3 with Certificate Pinning for All OTA/App Channels
scenes.Description: OTA client and app manager shall use TLS 1.3 with pinned leaf certificates. Certificate mismatch shall abort the connection and trigger a security alert DTC.

scenes.Name: [CS-IHU-R2] Apply Android Automotive OS SELinux Policy Hardening
scenes.Description: Remove all permissive SELinux domains. Audit and restrict all SUID/SGID binaries. Verify policy using automated policy analysis tool on each build.

scenes.Name: [CS-IHU-R3] Restrict USB Device Class Enumeration to Allowlist
scenes.Description: USB host driver shall only enumerate Audio (0x01), HID (0x03), and MTP (0xFF/0x00) device classes. All other classes shall be rejected at the driver level before any data transfer.

scenes.Name: [CS-IHU-R4] Implement CAN Gateway Domain-Isolation Allowlist
scenes.Description: CAN gateway firmware shall implement a static allowlist of permitted infotainment→vehicle message IDs. Unknown IDs shall be dropped. Overflow events shall be logged, rate-limited, and surfaced as DTC U0155.

scenes.Name: [CS-IHU-R5] Encrypt PII at Rest — AES-256-GCM with Device-Bound Key
scenes.Description: Contact lists, call history, SMS, and payment tokens shall be stored in an encrypted SQLite database using AES-256-GCM. The key shall be derived from a device-unique secret fused at manufacturing.

scenes.Name: [CS-IHU-R6] Isolate RIL Telephony Daemon in Namespaced Sandbox
scenes.Description: The telephony daemon shall run in a Linux PID/mount/network namespace with access only to /dev/modem and its own data partition. No IPC to CAN gateway or filesystem paths outside its domain shall be permitted.

scenes.Name: [CS-IHU-R7] Verify Navigation Map Merkle-Tree Hash Before Storage Commit
scenes.Description: Navigation app shall validate SHA-256 Merkle tree hash manifest (signed ECDSA-P256) before committing any tile update to /data/navi. Hash mismatch shall rollback update and log DTC.
